title: Build and Height
label: ch:ml-build
canDo: I can describe a person as short, thin or stout, and say that someone is tall.

payoff.summary: From cold: three adjectives that go in front of the noun, and one noun that cannot.
payoff.note: Four atoms. THE POINT'S NOTE WAS ACCURATE, verified before drafting for the second chapter running: valiya and cheriya are indeed the only size adjectives taught and they describe THINGS, and kuriya, melinja, thadicha, uyaram, pokkam, uyaramulla and neelamulla all return zero on a token-bounded sweep. TALL IS REACHED BY A DIFFERENT ROUTE, AND THAT IS THE CHAPTER'S POINT. Malayalam's ordinary word for tall is uyaramulla, which needs the relative participle uLLa -- and uLLa is taught NOWHERE in the corpus, zero occurrences. Rather than smuggle it in, the chapter teaches uyaram as a noun and reaches tall through the dative-existential the learner already owns: ML-C32-undu (650) states undu as 'there is / someone has' in as many words, and ML-C06-dative-subject (330) owns enikku. so enikku uyaramuNTu is built entirely from taught pieces. The lesson's literal gloss, 'to me height there-is', is the honest one: a bare dative-existential is nearer 'I have height' than the idiomatic tall, which usually carries a degree word, and pokkam is the commoner noun for a person's stature. The chapter claims what it can BUILD, not that it has built the idiom. The same refusal as ozhivusamayam in chapter 98 and dharikkuka here. NO NEW GRAMMAR: the three adjectives sit in ML-C42's frame, and uyaram's join is the anusvara taking its full letter BEFORE aaNu and undu -- scoped, because the first draft said the anusvara does that 'always, when something follows it', which ML-C96-eluppam and ML-C97-alla-sundaram both deny in as many words and which this chapter's OWN recall romanization refutes: uyaram + um is uyaravuM, with a va. THE REAL TEACHING IS THAT ADJACENT WORDS ARE NOT SYNONYMS -- cheriya and kuriya differ only in their FIRST SYLLABLE (che against ku, which is TWO characters, not one) and do not mean the same thing, small against short, and tall is the mirror of neither. REVIEW CORRECTED THE FIRST DRAFT OF THIS CLAIM, which said cheriya is for OBJECTS and kuriya for PEOPLE. That is false of both words AND it contradicted a merged lesson: ML-C42-small (1020) tells the learner to put cheriya 'in front of a word you already know', and by 1020 they own kutti (810) -- so the book had already invited cheriya kutti, which this chapter was about to declare impossible. TWO INVENTIONS WERE CAUGHT BEFORE THE FIRST COMMIT, both by a token sweep rather than by reading. aaL (person) was written into kuriya's example sentence and is taught NOWHERE; it became kutti, which is owned since 810 and whose weld the last three chapters have drilled. And sahOdaran was about to be quoted in Malayalam script from ML-C32-undu, which gives that example only in ROMANIZATION -- quoting it in script would have introduced an unowned word. The borrowed example was dropped instead. A WHOLE-TOKEN OWNER SWEEP is now run over every new file before commit: it lists every Malayalam token with no headword owner, leaving only joined forms built from owned pieces and metalinguistic ending fragments. Also corrected in draft: melinja's adjective list said 'every adjective so far' while omitting nalla.
